[/page/0/Text/7] This study aimed to explore how the life history of suicide victims with no history of treatment in mental health care or of attempted suicide seemed to presdispose them to maladaptive perfectionism. Three main themes emerged: (a) exposure to high expectations combined with little recognition and warmth; (b) reduced ability to cope with failures and weaknesses; and (c) fear of emotional rejection. Together these themes illustrate that feelings of shame, mainly resulting from an unfulfilled need for attachment, a desire for love and recognition may relate to maladaptive perfectionism, which influences the suicidal process.

Perfectionism seemed to be an important element in the suicides of six men with no history of attempted suicide or treatment in mental health care. Striving for success was the life project of these men, associated with a fear of failure and a strong urge to keep up the fac¸ade. This combined with rigidity, made these men unable to cope with self-experienced failures or adapt to significant negative life events. They seemed to have experienced failures as an irreversible defeat, and eventually suicide became their "solution."

Three main themes predisposing the individuals to maladaptive perfectionism related to suicide, emerged from the analysis of the life history of the six men in the present material: (a) Exposure to high expectations combined with little recognition and warmth; (b) Reduced ability to cope with failures and weaknesses; and (c) Fear of emotional rejection.

evidence.section_title: Exposure to High Expectations Combined With Little Recognition and Warmth
evidence.quote: [/page/8/Text/7] The deceased were understood as perfectionists based upon their strong engagement in work, study, and career and were perceived to be very successful and well-functioning men. [/page/8/Text/8] However, in their narratives, informants clearly perceived that the parents' unrealistic expectations and their concern about fac¸ade and status went beyond what their sons' could live up to. [/page/9/Text/4] Furthermore, a common pattern that emerged in the informants narratives was the lack of recognition from the father of the deceased. [/page/10/Text/5] According to informants other than parents, repeated experiences of defeat and lack of recognition during childhood and adolescence may have led the deceased to repair this emotional damage by being successful. Thus, life became a struggle for achieving, in order to gain admiration.

evidence.section_title: Reduced Ability to Cope With Failures and Weaknesses
evidence.quote: [/page/10/Text/7] Feelings of failure and weakness in youth and adulthood seemed to predispose these men to perfectionist behavior. [/page/11/Text/4] Consequently, this discrepancy may have further reduced the deceased's ability to cope with failures and weaknesses in life and may have propelled the deceased to work even harder, and in short, pushed them further toward maladaptive perfectionism.

Furthermore, all love relationships in four cases related the deceased's tendency towards perfectionism to negative emotional experiences, associated with a one way communication between the deceased and their parents (in particular their fathers) where these negative experiences were not addressed.

Risk: "The developmental history of the deceased revealed how negative experiences during their upbringing may have predisposed these men to develop maladaptive perfectionism as adults." [page/13/Text/6], "Maladaptive perfectionism seems to be related to an unsolved dependency of being recognized, especially by fathers (or father figures) who neglected and/or rejected the deceased's needs." [page/13/Text/6], "The present study suggests that most of the fathers may have played the major role in socializing their sons into a stereotypic gender role pattern. In this context, the developmental history of the men in the present study may thus be interpreted as an indication of masculinity in the sense that the deceased were less able to address and handle social defeats, and address negative emotional experiences" [page/14/Text/4], "Our findings related perfectionist tendencies to a history of emotional vulnerability such as shame and humiliation." [page/14/Text/5], "Maladaptive perfectionism among these six men may have originated from shame and humiliation, being the result of unfinished issues/needs for attachment, a desire for autonomy, and an urge to be loved and recognized." [page/14/Text/7]. Recovery: "However, prevention of suicide related to maladaptive perfectionism may basically consist of two strategies: (a) prevent suicide among people who already are maladaptive perfectionists and (b) prevent maladaptive perfectionism among young people. Strategies should include an increased focus upon childrens' upbringing." [page/15/Text/4], "In particular, perfectionistic young people should be encouraged to be more open and be helped to believe in the positive feedback they receive from their supportive social networks, as well as being encouraged to seek professional help if needed. Increasing self-esteem through trust in the self and their own values as opposed to external values is of importance." [page/16/Text/2]
